Title: cookies are not correctly set for hostnames with ports

Related to https://github.com/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy/issues/2055

Currently, the following code will print the warning `Warning: request host %q did not match any of the specific cookie domains of %q` and default to the shortest domain when the hostname of a request and cookie are not matched:

https://github.com/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy/blob/dd4fa414eadb065f0d0c38d9b21421c333f88b98/pkg/cookies/cookies.go#L19-L26

However, this is NOT the correct behavior (and may result in setting the cookie on the incorrect domain), because as discussed in [this stack overflow thread](https://stackoverflow.com/a/4212964/5030772), browsers do not distinguish the ports of cookies.

Therefore, we should be stripping off any `:XXXX` port suffix from the request host when checking which cookie_domain to match it to.

Title: OIDC provider fails to retrieve claim (ADFS backend)

## Expected Behavior

The OIDC provider is expected to work with an ADFS backend providing v1.0 ID tokens. It did work in version 7.2.1.

## Current Behavior

Disclaimer: Im neither an OIDC nor a Go expert, but this is what I found out:

When the OIDC provider fails to extract the claim `preferred_username` from the ID token (which is not present in v1.0 tokens according to specification), it tries to fetch it by making a request to the profile URL. This request fails with code 401 in my case:

`Error redeeming code during OAuth2 callback: could not get claim "preferred_username": failed to fetch claims from profile URL: error making request to profile URL: unexpected status "401":`

Apparently, this behaviour was introduced with 9670513 and could explain some of the issues described in #1666 and https://github.com/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy/issues/1715#issuecomment-1367957338.

## Possible Solution

It should either be possible to skip extraction of the `preferred_username` claim via configuration or to disable the profile URL request altogether (setting `--profile-url` to `""` does not work because the URL is discovered automatically).

## Your Environment

- Microsoft ADFS server (set up to be used as an Open ID provider)
- Version of oauth2-proxy used: 7.3.0, 7.5.1

GitLab provider is unusable because access token timeout is 2m and refresh flow will always fail. Thus, the maximum amount of time a valid session can be sustained is < 2m.

## Expected Behavior
ID token verification should pass if the token is signed with ES256 (bug)

This works fine when the prebuilt docker image [quay.io/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy](https://quay.io/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy) is used. It fails with the latest code changes.

ID token verification is failing with the following error:
[2022/04/22 11:34:24] [oauthproxy.go:768] Error redeeming code during OAuth2 callback: could not verify id_token: failed to verify token: oidc: id token signed with unsupported algorithm, expected ["RS256"] got "ES256"

Investigated this a bit, seems like it might be related to changes in OIDC discovery code (https://github.com/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy/pull/1559)

```
	supportedSigAlgs := v.config.SupportedSigningAlgs
	if len(supportedSigAlgs) == 0 {
		supportedSigAlgs = []string{RS256}
	}

	if !contains(supportedSigAlgs, sig.Header.Algorithm) {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("oidc: id token signed with unsupported algorithm, expected %q got %q", supportedSigAlgs, sig.Header.Algorithm)
	}
```

However, it fails to verify the id_token

Trying to use the latest code, since PKCE is needed for our use-case.
Provider configuration cannot be changed to sign id_token with RS256, hence this is a blocking issue.

When the EKS OIDC provider rotates it's keys the OAuth2 proxy/go-oidc client does not update it's key set causing some tokens to fail with: "Error retrieving session from token in Authorization header: unable to verify jwt token". The key ID from the failing token matches exactly with the freshly added key.

## Expected Behavior

OAuth2 proxy key set should be in sync with the EKS OIDC provider, so that all service account token can be validated.

## Current Behavior

The EKS OIDC provider returns "cache-control: max-age=604800" in the http header, go-oidc sets 7 days expiration for each remoteKeySet and does NOT fetch keys even if it cannot find a key in the remoteKeySet meaning that authenticated using a token generated from freshly rotated keys fails with: "Error retrieving session from token in Authorization header: unable to verify jwt token".

## Possible Solution

version v2.2.1 of go-oidc library contains a [bug](https://github.com/coreos/go-oidc/pull/259) regarding key rotation strategy which has been solved in v3.0.0, upgrade dependency.

## Version used
 v6.1.1 (master uses the same go-oidc version), we've now upgraded to v7.1.3 in preparation for a patch release.

Title: Support PROXY Protocol

I propose to implement support for the PROXY protocol in OAuth2-Proxy. That would make it possible to run OAuth2-Proxy behind a L7 load balancer or reverse proxy, but without the requirement of having the LB/proxy decrypt the TLS connection.

## Current Behavior

When running OAuth2-Proxy behind a load balancer or reverse proxy, the LB/proxy needs to be able to terminate/decrypt the TLS connection to inject the `X-Forwarded-For` headers and thereby inform OAuth2-Proxy of the client's actual IP address. (Though I haven't tried it, the documentation suggests OAuth2-Proxy already supports this kind of setup.) Because of this requirement, the LB/proxy can see all traffic going to OAuth2-Proxy in plain text, which is a bit of a security risk.

## Expected Behavior

There is an alternative to injecting `X-Forwarded-For` and similar headers into the (otherwise encrypted) HTTP request: the [PROXY protocol](https://www.haproxy.org/download/1.8/doc/proxy-protocol.txt). Effectively, it works be prefixing a bit of information to the TCP datastream. (Depending on the version of the protocol, the information is prefixed either in plain ASCII text or in a binary format.)

It would be nice if OAuth2-Proxy supported this protocol. This way, one could run OAuth2-Proxy behind a load balancer or reverse proxy without giving the LB/proxy the necessary TLS keys (and thereby full access to the plaintext HTTP traffic). Of course, the load balancer needs to support the proxy protocol, too.

## Possible Solution

Googling for support of the PROXY protocol in Go came up with a number of implementations:
* https://inkel.github.io/posts/proxy-protocol/ / https://github.com/inkel/viaproxy
* https://github.com/sprucehealth/go-proxy-protocol
* https://github.com/armon/go-proxyproto
* https://github.com/pires/go-proxyproto

The first ones appear to be quite basic (but also short) implementations. The last one appears to be the most complete and actively maintained one.

## Context




My goal would be to set up OAuth2-Proxy:
* behind a load balancer
* in a way such that OAuth2-Proxy has the real client's IP address
* in a way such that the load balancer doesn't need to have the TLS keys to decrypt the incoming traffic.

## Your Environment

- Version used: 7.3.0
- load balancer
- Kubernetes

Title: cookie-csrf-per-request: allow setting maximum number of csrf cookies

## Expected Behavior
In order to allow a user to sign in from multiple tabs simultaneously the cookie-csrf-per-request setting can be set to true. This adds a random postfix to the csrf cookie with each request. This causes a problem for us as many apps will do http calls using javascript fetch or XHR, and the browser does not follow the 302 redirects to the openid provider sent by oauth2-proxy in response. After enough calls (even with a shorter csrf cookie lifetime) we end up with a 'request header too large' 431 status code as each csrf cookie is quite large.

I suggest setting a maximum number of csrf cookies to prevent this behavior. OAuth2-proxy will, when faced with an incoming request with more than this number of csrf cookies, respond by removing the oldest `size(cookies) - cookielimit` cookies. 



## Current Behavior
OAuth2-proxy simply adds a new cookie for every single request, which very quickly leads to very large request headers size, causing most reverse proxies and servers to respond with a 431 request header too large status code.



## Possible Solution
When an incoming request (that is not part of the openid connect flow) has more csrf cookies than the configured limit, unset the oldest csrf cookies. The main challenge here is figuring out which csrf cookie is the oldest, as I'm not sure the cookie contains this information. 

I suggest leaving the default unlimited to prevent breaking changes in the behavior of oauth2-proxy.





## Context
Our users regularly end up with the 431 status code response. We have already lowered the csrf cookie lifetime to 5 minutes, but sometimes an app simply sends a boatload of http requests in a short period and ends up generating a lot of csrf cookies. We hope setting a limit on the number of cookies will still allow users to sign in from multiple tabs (we had frequent 500 errors as the cookie no longer matched before enabling cookie-csrf-per-request), but will in almost all cases prevent 431 status codes with a reasonable request header limit on our reverse proxy.



## Your Environment



- Version used: 7.5.1-debian-11-r14 (from bitnami)
- incoming http requests are intercepted by Istio service mesh and sent to oauth2-proxy, though this issue likely exists even when using oauth2-proxy for only a single app

Title: Include PKCE - Code Challenge in Proxy (2nd try)

## Expected Behavior

For security reasons It would be nice if the PKCE extension would be included in the proxy.
https://www.oauth.com/oauth2-servers/pkce/. 

This was already requested in https://github.com/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy/issues/756 but I think the discussion was not considering the latest OAuth2 spec (see https://oauth.net/2.1/): _PKCE is required for all OAuth clients using the authorization code flow_. 
That means also for confidential clients and not only for mobile and SPA clients as @etca2z stated before. So using PKCE is state of the art for me and I want to use PKCE.

```
https://YOUR_DOMAIN/authorize?
    response_type=code&
    code_challenge=CODE_CHALLENGE&
    code_challenge_method=S256&
    client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&
    redirect_uri=YOUR_CALLBACK_URL&
    scope=SCOPE&
    state=STATE
```
In contrast to the code flow without PKCE  a code_challenge has to be submitted. I think this is not done currently in the code, see https://github.com/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy/blob/06808704a3762de73bed1cc92b077420eb93d735/providers/util.go#L38

To follow the 2.1 spec regarding PKCE I think oauth2-proxy should handle the PKCE flow.

PS:  since I can see different abbreviations in  #756: I'm talking about PKCE - Proof Key for Code Exchange, see https://auth0.com/docs/flows/authorization-code-flow-with-proof-key-for-code-exchange-pkce. It's not related to PKCS or PKSE (?) in this context.

## Current Behavior

PKCE cannot be used for the authorization and callback request

## Possible Solution

It would be good if it could be enabled by a property.

Title: Support for direct access (aka resource owner) grant ?

Hi,

I'm quite new to oauth2 and oauth2_proxy. I use oauth2_proxy with keycloak and nginx and I'm very happy with it as long as we stay in a browser.

I have some http APIs I would like to authenticate through a proxy with basic authentication or opaque tokens using existing keycloak IDP. Typically users use CLI tools (curl / others) to request APIs, some of them doesn't supports other authentication than basic auth.

In oauth2 specification, there's a direct access grant, also called resource owner credential grant. For a auth2 client (like the proxy) this mean we can issue jwt token with a POST request on ``/token`` and passing ``grant_type=password``, ``client_id=xxx``, ``client_secret=xxx``, ``username=jdoe``, ``password=secret``.

So the proxy could have a endpoint like ``/oauth2/auth`` (suitable for nginx auth_request) accepting basic auth (username, password), authenticate by issuing a jwt token and return "200 OK" or "401 Unauthorized". Eventually he could also cache a hash of user/password for a reasonable time. And to avoid sending user/password, maybe also issue opaque tokens for end-user application supporting it.

By reading the documentation, looks there's some options about basic-auth / authorization header but by reading the code I didn't see a support for ``grant_type=password``.

Also note that I'm not sure this is the correct way to handle such "legacy" applications with a proxy.

Thanks for answers!
